== Research Notes ==

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. Adam D. Glasgow of Broughshane appears in the Royal Belfast Academical Institution school prizes in June 1830 and Belfast College examinations reported in May 1831. The 1831 report also names James Glasgow, Institution, in voluntary advanced mathematical examinations.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 29 June 1830, p.3, Royal Belfast Academical Institution School Department; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390569859/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 6 May 1831, p.3, Belfast College report dated 30 April; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390545285/ record].</ref> [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] and James McClure [[Glasgow-1780]] are strong compatible candidates. The newspaper gives no ages or parents and does not call these men brothers. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. The 2 May 1828 award list separately names Jas. Glasgow of Broughshane in the Junior Division and James Glasgow in the Logic and Belles Lettres section. The 1 May 1830 report lists James Glasgow of the Institution for senior-course voluntary mathematics and a premium for the third book of Locke’s Essay.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 9 May 1828, p.3, Belfast Institution College Department, awards on 2 May; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390546969/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 7 May 1830, p.2, Belfast College report dated 1 May; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390568607/ record].</ref> The two 1828 entries are distinct mentions; whether they refer to one student or two remains unresolved. [[Glasgow-1780]] remains a strong compatible candidate for the wider Institution, teaching and ministry sequence, but this award list alone does not establish the 1828 identity. These notices give no age, full middle name, parents or spouse; they establish no sibling relationship. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. James Glasgow, Institution, received the silver medal for general-certificate examinations in mathematics and natural philosophy at the College Department awards on 28 April 1832. On 11 December 1834 pupils presented Rev. James Glasgow with a watch on his resignation as principal assistant in the Institution’s Mathematical and Mercantile School. He was an assistant, not its principal.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 4 May 1832, p.3, Institution College Department awards of 28 April; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390568466/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 12 December 1834, p.2, Royal Institution—Mr Glasgow, assistant resignation; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390561231/ record].</ref> The Society secretary comparison remains unproved. The 1834 newspaper’s Rev. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. Castledawson’s unanimous call to Rev. James Glasgow had already been reported by 10 July 1835. His ordination to its pastoral charge took place on Tuesday 6 October 1835, reported on 16 October. The current James McClure [[Glasgow-1780]] biography labels 6 October as his call date; a sourced correction is prepared locally.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 10 July 1835, p.2, Castledawson unanimous call; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390571333/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 16 October 1835, p.2, Castledawson ordination on 6 October; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390573717/ record].</ref> The exact call date is unstated; 6 October is explicitly the ordination date. Rev. Mr Wallace of Rasharkin preached, Rev. Mr Rogers of Kilrea handled the defence of Presbyterian ordination, and Rev. Mr Elder of Finvoy offered the ordination prayer. Their presence is not kinship or proof that James lived in Rasharkin/Kilrea/Finvoy. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. Margaret Jane, infant daughter of Rev. James Glasgow, missionary to Kattywar for the Presbyterian Church in Ireland, died at Rajkote, East Indies, on 11 June 1841, aged two months and 26 days.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 10 September 1841, p.2, Margaret Jane Glasgow death notice; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390562197/ record].</ref> Strong matching name, father, place and date support [[Glasgow-2898]] and her father [[Glasgow-1780]]. The notice does not name her mother or birthplace. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. At Surat, East Indies, the wife of Rev. James Glasgow, Presbyterian Church in Ireland missionary, gave birth to a daughter on 22 February, reported on 11 April 1848. The child and mother are unnamed. Annie Coulson [[Glasgow-2901|Glasgow]], whose birth is placed in India in 1848, is a possible identification of the daughter.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 11 April 1848, p.2, Surat birth on 22 February; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390546223/ record].</ref> 1848 is inferred from the contemporary notice’s February date. Neither child nor mother is named. The notice cannot alone make Annie’s exact birth date/place certain or establish Mary Wightman’s motherhood of another child. Her existing father/mother connections are not changed. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. The report describes the ordination of Rev. Samuel Smith to the Draperstown congregation by the Presbytery of Magherafelt on Tuesday 28 March 1837. After the service, the congregation entertained the Presbytery and friends at dinner. In its account of the gathering, it names Rev. J. Glasgow of Castledawson among the other speakers.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 1837-04-04, p.4; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390545495/ record].</ref> The printed name is Rev. J. Glasgow, not an expanded full name. Castledawson and the ministerial context make James McClure [[Glasgow-1780]] a probable compatible candidate for this record within the already supported career sequence; the newspaper alone does not establish that full identity. The report does not change the pending call-date or ordination-date review, and no family relationship is inferred. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. The 5 April 1842 Belfast News-Letter passage invokes “Glasgow in India” in a comparison of missionary and clerical conduct in the Indies and Ireland. It names no forename and describes no particular event.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 5 April 1842, p.1; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390554509/ record].</ref> The surrounding passage treats Glasgow as an individual missionary in India, not a place. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. Under Marriages, the 1 July 1840 notice reports that “On Saturday last, the Rev. James Glasgow, of Castledawson, in the county Derry,” married Miss Mary Wightman of Belfast.<ref>Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 1 July 1840, p.2, marriage notice; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050113101/ record].</ref> The event date is inferred as 27 June 1840 from “Saturday last”; that date was Saturday. The newspaper does not give his middle name. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. The report “Designation of Four Missionaries of the General Assembly” says that the Presbytery of Belfast set apart four ministers as fellow-labourers in Hindostan with Rev. James Glasgow: Rev. Adam Glasgow, James M’Kee, Robert Montgomery, and James Henry Spears. The service was held Wednesday at Dr Cooke’s church, May Street, Belfast.<ref>Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 14 January 1842, p.1, designation of four missionaries; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050136610/ record].</ref> James McClure [[Glasgow-1780]] is a probable compatible candidate for Rev. James Glasgow from his documented Presbyterian Church in Ireland missionary career. [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] is a possible compatible candidate for Rev. These co-mentioned ministers are not thereby shown to be relatives. This is a missionary report, separate from the adjacent Repeal Association text. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. The same 18 August 1840 soiree report separately says the gathering was addressed by “the Rev. James Glasgow, Missionary to India.” This is a distinct named person and role from Rev. Adam Glasgow.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 21 August 1840, p. 2, Rev. James Glasgow, Missionary to India (separate passage); [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560975/ record].</ref> James Glasgow is named “Missionary to India.” This is a separate man/role from Rev. Adam Glasgow; it is compatible with, but does not uniquely identify, [[Glasgow-1780]]. No kinship with Rev. Adam is inferred from their co-occurrence in the soiree report. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. “Belfast College,” dated 1 May 1829, reports that premiums were distributed at the close of the session. Under “For Essays proposed to the Logic Class of last year,” it lists “On the Application of Testimony to Miraculous Events, James Glasgow, Belfast College.” James is listed as the essay award recipient, not as the proposer of the topic. The same page also has a separate geographic “near Glasgow” and a separate James M’Clatchey.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 5 May 1829, p. 3, Belfast College essay premium; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390581832/ record].</ref> The named Belfast College student is a possible match to [[Glasgow-1780]] by the broader education-to-ministry sequence only; this notice alone does not identify him as the later Castledawson minister. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. Under ‘Ordination At Bellaghy,’ the report says the Magherafelt Presbytery ordained Rev. Gilbert Kirker Wilson to Bellaghy on ‘the 15th ult.’ Rev. James Glasgow, of Castledawson, commenced the service with a sermon. After the report of the service, the same account describes the toasts: the chairman gave ‘The Gentlemen who officiated this day,’ and Rev. James Glasgow returned thanks. With the 5 April issue date, ‘15th ult.’ means 15 March 1836.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 5 April 1836, p. 4, Bellaghy ordination; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390544149/ record].</ref> A contemporaneous Castledawson ministerial occurrence, compatible with [[Glasgow-1780]] in the established career sequence; the source does not state his middle name or family. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. In the General Assembly report, “The Assembly then proceeded to set apart two Missionaries to India—namely, the Rev. James Glasgow, of Castledawson, and the Rev. Alexander Kerr, of Portadown.” They stated their motives and were set apart for the India mission. No exact meeting date is supplied in this excerpt. Elsewhere on the same page, a separate report says two Synod ministers, Messrs. Adam Glasgow and James Carr, offered for the Synod’s foreign mission to India; this is a distinct passage and establishes no relationship to James.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 14 July 1840, p. 1, India missionary appointment; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390559244/ record].</ref> Castledawson and India mission career are probable matches to [[Glasgow-1780]] as a continuing subject; the printed source does not state a middle name. Adam Glasgow in a separate earlier clause is a separate person occurrence; no kinship is inferred. The printed line breaks the place across lines as “Porta-/down,” read as Portadown. The place is printed across a line break as “Porta-/down,” read as Portadown. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. Under “The General Assembly’S Missionaries In India,” a report says a very interesting letter had been received “from the Rev. James Glasgow, by Mrs. Wilson, of Townsend-street,” about the sale of two boxes of ladies’ work sent from Derry and Belfast to Bombay; about 500 rupees (£50) was realised. The issue date is 25 May 1841; this excerpt does not give the letter’s date.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 25 May 1841, p. 4, India mission letter report; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390558896/ record].</ref> The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. Under “General Assembly’S Foreign Mission—Sickness And Death Of The Rev. A. Kerr,” the newspaper says a communication from Rev. Mr. Glasgow was read about fellow missionary Alexander Kerr. The letter is dated “Rajkote, 14th August, 1841” and is signed “James Glasgow.” In this context “brother missionary” means colleague/fellow worker, not a biological brother. A separate letter dated 18 August follows; its author is not established by the inspected passage.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 19 October 1841, p. 2, Rajkote letter on Alexander Kerr; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390563026/ record].</ref> The signed India-mission letter is a probable match to [[Glasgow-1780]] in the established career sequence. The letter’s date (14 August) is separate from the newspaper publication date (19 October). The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Institution student / assistant and Castledawson minister, 1828–1848. A separate editorial passage says: “The Rev. James Glasgow is much to be envied. The first Moderator of the first Indian Presbytery—he who stood alone among millions of heathens—will occupy an honoured page in the history of Christian missions.” Publication date is 29 July 1842. The same issue separately prints a letter by Rev. Adam Glasgow, datelined Rajkote, 16 May 1842; that date belongs to Adam’s letter, not to the James editorial.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 29 July 1842, p. 2, first Indian Presbytery moderator; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390558014/ record].</ref> The named James is a probable match to [[Glasgow-1780]] in the documented Castledawson/India missionary sequence. The editorial supplies no full middle name or kinship statement; Adam’s adjacent letter is a distinct source passage. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Belfast Juvenile Society secretary, 1830–1831. James Glasgow and Walter Moffat are named secretaries announcing the Belfast Juvenile Society’s sixth annual meeting at Rev. Dr Cooke’s May Street meeting-house on Monday 15 November 1830. In March 1831 Rev. Walter Moffatt and Mr James Glasgow attended a Knockbracken meeting as the Society’s deputation; Rev. Thomas Houston chaired it.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 12 November 1830, p.2, Belfast Juvenile Society sixth annual meeting announcement; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390573239/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 4 March 1831, p.4, Belfast Juvenile Society, Knockbracken meeting; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390543442/ record].</ref> The repeated society and associates support one society account. The same Walter Moffat appears in the 1828 Institution report, making [[Glasgow-1780]] a compatible student/ministry-network candidate; this does not prove that the society secretary is the college student. The newspaper does not call James the president, chair or minister. The identification remains uncertain.
